title: Chapter 3 — Designing Good Data Architecture: Quality Question Bank

questions.question: Using Bezos's "one-way door / two-way door" framework as the book presents it, how would shutting down AWS entirely compare to requiring a new microservice to use DynamoDB?
options: Shutting down AWS is a one-way door (nearly impossible to reverse); mandating DynamoDB for one service is a two-way door (easily reversible)
Both are one-way doors, since cloud infrastructure decisions are always irreversible
Shutting down AWS is a two-way door; mandating DynamoDB is a one-way door
Both are two-way doors, since any technology decision can eventually be undone
questions.explanation: The book gives exactly these two examples: shutting down AWS would be nearly impossible to reverse (one-way door), while requiring DynamoDB for a new service could be reversed by refactoring (two-way door).

questions.question: What is the book's own working definition of data architecture?
options: A fixed blueprint of all data systems that should not change once approved
A department responsible for enforcing data governance policy
The set of ETL tools and pipelines used to move data between systems
The design of systems to support the evolving data needs of an enterprise, achieved by flexible and reversible decisions reached through careful evaluation of trade-offs
questions.explanation: This is stated verbatim as the authors' definition, built on their enterprise architecture definition and emphasizing flexibility, reversibility, and trade-offs — not a static, fixed blueprint.

questions.question: What's the difference between operational and technical data architecture, per the book?
options: Operational and technical architecture are two names for the same concept
Operational architecture applies only to cloud systems; technical architecture applies only to on-premises systems

Operational architecture describes the functional requirements (people, process, technology) — what needs to happen; technical architecture describes how data is ingested, stored, transformed, and served
Operational architecture is the concern of data scientists exclusively; technical architecture is for data engineers exclusively
questions.explanation: The book states plainly: "operational architecture describes what needs to be done, and technical architecture details how it will happen."

questions.question: A team sets a five-minute recovery time objective (RTO) for their public e-commerce site, but a one-day RTO for an internal weekly reporting tool. Why does the book consider this appropriate?
options: RTO should reflect actual business impact: a brief e-commerce outage has major revenue impact, while a delayed internal report may be tolerable
RTO only applies to streaming systems, never to batch reporting tools
RTO must always be identical across every system for consistency
A shorter RTO always means lower infrastructure cost, so it should be minimized everywhere
questions.explanation: The book's own examples make this exact point: "An RTO of one day might be fine for an internal reporting system. A website outage of just five minutes could have a significant adverse business impact."

questions.question: How does the book distinguish recovery time objective (RTO) from recovery point objective (RPO)?
options: RTO measures data loss; RPO measures downtime
RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime for a service; RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss after recovery
RTO applies only to hardware failures; RPO applies only to software bugs
RTO and RPO measure the same thing, just under different vendor naming conventions
questions.explanation: The book defines RTO as "the maximum acceptable time for a service or system outage" and RPO as "the maximum acceptable data loss" after recovery — two distinct dimensions of failure planning.

questions.question: What does it mean for a system to "scale to zero," as the book describes it?
options: It guarantees zero downtime under all conditions
It can shut down completely when not in use, as many serverless functions and serverless OLAP databases do automatically
It requires zero ongoing maintenance from engineers
Its storage costs are always zero, regardless of data volume
questions.explanation: The book gives this exact definition: some scalable systems "can also scale to zero: they shut down completely when not in use," citing serverless functions and serverless OLAP databases as examples.

questions.question: Amazon's 2002 "API Mandate" is used in the book as an example of building loosely coupled systems. What was its core rule, and what did it enable?
options: All teams had to standardize on a single programming language for consistency
All teams had to store their data in one shared central database for simplicity
All teams needed sign-off from a central architecture committee before shipping
All teams must expose data/functionality only through service interfaces, with no direct database reads or shared memory allowed — this loose coupling eventually enabled AWS
questions.explanation: The mandate required all interprocess communication to go through service interfaces ("no direct linking, no direct reads of another team's data store... no back-doors whatsoever"), which the book credits with enabling the loose coupling that led to AWS.

questions.question: How does the book contrast the traditional hardened-perimeter security model with the zero-trust, shared-responsibility approach used in the cloud?
options: Hardened-perimeter assumes everything inside the network boundary is trustworthy (vulnerable to insider threats/phishing); in the cloud, responsibility instead splits between the provider (security ‘of’ the cloud) and the customer (security ‘in’ the cloud)
The hardened-perimeter model is only relevant to streaming architectures
Zero trust eliminates any need for encryption
Zero trust means the cloud provider is solely responsible for all security, with no customer role
questions.explanation: The book illustrates the hardened-perimeter model's weakness to insider threats (the Mission Impossible example), then contrasts it with AWS's shared responsibility model splitting security ‘of’ vs ‘in’ the cloud.

questions.question: Why does the book argue "all data engineers should consider themselves security engineers"?
options: The cloud pushes security responsibility to engineers outside dedicated security roles, and real breaches (like public S3 buckets) have resulted from this responsibility being ignored
It means only engineers formally on a security team may configure cloud storage
It means data engineers must hold a formal security certification before touching any pipeline
It means data engineers should always encrypt every dataset twice for redundancy
questions.explanation: The book notes the cloud "pushes this responsibility out to engineers who are not explicitly in security roles," and cites real S3-misconfiguration breaches as the consequence of ignoring it.

questions.question: FinOps, as the book describes it, brings engineering together with which discipline, and to manage what?
options: Finance — to manage dynamic, pay-as-you-go cloud spending collaboratively and with data-driven decisions, replacing fixed capital-expenditure budgeting
HR — to manage data team headcount costs
Marketing — to manage customer acquisition costs
Legal — to manage data-privacy compliance costs
questions.explanation: The book quotes the FinOps Foundation's definition directly: a "cloud financial management discipline" enabling engineering, finance, technology, and business teams to collaborate on data-driven spending decisions.

questions.question: A company's sales domain creates invoices, and its accounting domain must track those same invoices to ensure payment. How does the book suggest structuring this?
options: A single centralized "finance" domain should absorb both sales and accounting
Accounting should own all invoice data exclusively, with sales having no access at all
Sales and accounting each own their respective domain, but share a common "invoice" service between them
Each domain should maintain its own fully duplicated copy of invoice data
questions.explanation: This is the book's own worked example: "the accounting domain shares the invoice service with the sales domain since a sale generates an invoice... Sales and accounting own their respective domains."

questions.question: How does the book distinguish vertical from horizontal scaling, and which does it say offers higher availability and reliability?
options: Horizontal scaling adds resources to a single machine; vertical scaling adds more machines

Vertical scaling adds resources to a single machine with hard limits and a single point of failure; horizontal scaling adds more machines, offering higher availability and reliability through distribution and redundancy
Both approaches offer identical reliability since they scale the same underlying hardware
Vertical scaling only applies to streaming systems, horizontal only to batch systems
questions.explanation: The book notes single machines (vertical scaling) "generally can't offer high availability and reliability," and that distributed, horizontally-scaled systems achieve this through added machines and built-in redundancy.

questions.question: A startup builds their MVP on a single server hosting both the database and application, to move fast under a deadline. What does the book say about this choice?
options: Single-tier architectures are always production-ready once a load balancer is added
It's fine for prototyping and development, but not advised for production, since a failure in the server, database, or application takes down the whole architecture
Single-tier architecture is specifically designed for high-concurrency production analytics
The book says single-tier architecture is never an acceptable choice at any stage
questions.explanation: The book states single-tier architectures "are good for prototyping and development, [but] they are not advised for production environments because of the obvious failure risks."

questions.question: How does the book contrast monolith and microservices architectures in terms of failure behavior?
options: Microservices architectures guarantee zero downtime by design
Monoliths are always more reliable because there's only one system to monitor

In a monolith, tight coupling means a change or failure in one area can ripple elsewhere ("whack-a-mole"); in microservices, one service going down temporarily doesn't stop other loosely coupled services from functioning
Monoliths and microservices have identical failure-isolation properties
questions.explanation: The book describes improving a monolith as "a game of whack-a-mole," while for microservices: "If one service temporarily goes down, it won't affect the ability of other services to continue functioning."

questions.question: Under AWS's shared responsibility model as the book describes it, who is responsible for "security of the cloud" versus "security in the cloud"?
options: Security of the cloud and security in the cloud are the same responsibility, just described from two angles
AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud (the infrastructure running its services); the customer is responsible for security IN the cloud (correctly configuring their own use of those services)
The customer is responsible for both, regardless of provider
AWS is responsible for both, regardless of customer configuration
questions.explanation: The book quotes AWS directly: AWS "is responsible for protecting the infrastructure that runs AWS services," while "your responsibility is determined by the AWS service that you use" — i.e. security in the cloud.

questions.question: What is the key architectural difference between Lambda and Kappa architecture for unifying batch and streaming data?
options: Lambda and Kappa are simply two names for the same architecture

Lambda runs separate batch, streaming, and serving systems that must be reconciled; Kappa uses a single stream-processing platform as the backbone for all data handling, replaying the stream for batch-like needs
Lambda uses only streaming pipelines; Kappa uses only batch pipelines
Kappa requires a separate speed layer and batch layer, while Lambda does not
questions.explanation: The book describes Lambda as running batch, streaming, and serving as independent systems requiring reconciliation, while Kappa's premise is "why not just use a stream-processing platform as the backbone for all data handling."

questions.question: What problems does the book associate with first-generation ("1.0") data lakes?
options: They required proprietary hardware only large enterprises could afford
They could only store structured relational data, not unstructured data
They often became unmanaged "data swamps" with poor schema/cataloging, painful deletes/updates, ballooning Hadoop-cluster costs, and a write-only design that clashed with regulations like GDPR
They were prohibitively expensive to set up and offered no cost advantage over data warehouses
questions.explanation: The book describes data lake 1.0's shortcomings in detail: the data swamp problem, DML operations that were "painful to implement," ballooning Hadoop costs, and a write-only design that clashed with GDPR's deletion requirements.

questions.question: What key capability does a data lakehouse add on top of a traditional data lake, per the book?
options: It removes the need for object storage, moving everything to local disks
It only supports structured data, unlike a data lake
Data-warehouse-style controls and data management on object storage — notably ACID transactions — unlike the original data lake's essentially write-only design
It eliminates the need for any query engine entirely
questions.explanation: The book says the lakehouse "supports atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability (ACID) transactions, a big departure from the original data lake, where you simply pour in data and never update or delete it."

questions.question: According to Zhamak Dehghani as cited in the book, what are the four key components of a data mesh?
options: Security, DataOps, orchestration, and software engineering
Domain-oriented decentralized data ownership and architecture, data as a product, self-serve data infrastructure as a platform, and federated computational governance
Data warehousing, data lakes, ETL, and reverse ETL
Centralized data ownership, data as a service, vendor-managed infrastructure, and command-and-control governance
questions.explanation: The book lists these four components exactly as identified by Dehghani, whose core idea is decentralizing away from a single centrally-owned data platform toward domain ownership.

questions.question: A team wants to migrate off a legacy monolith but worries a full rewrite is too risky. What approach does the book recommend, and why?
options: Jump straight to a greenfield project and abandon the legacy system without any migration plan
Always do a complete big-bang rewrite to get a clean slate
Never attempt to replace legacy systems, since deprecation is never worth the effort
The strangler pattern — incrementally replacing pieces of the legacy system over time — because it's targeted and supports flexible, reversible decisions, unlike a risky “big-bang” rewrite
questions.explanation: The book explicitly warns against "big-bang" overhauls ("this path often leads to disaster") and recommends the strangler pattern for its "targeted and surgical approach" that preserves reversibility.

questions.question: What is enterprise architecture in the chapter's working definition?
options: A fixed inventory of every application and database that must never change.
The design of systems to support change in the enterprise through flexible and reversible decisions and careful trade-off evaluation.
A governance committee responsible for approving all software purchases.
A collection of data pipelines used only by the data engineering team.
questions.explanation: The chapter defines enterprise architecture around supporting change through flexible, reversible decisions and trade-off evaluation.

questions.question: Which statement best describes how data architecture relates to enterprise architecture?
options: They are unrelated disciplines.
Data architecture replaces enterprise architecture in data-driven companies.
Data architecture is a subset of enterprise architecture.
Enterprise architecture is a subset of data architecture.
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly positions data architecture as a subset of enterprise architecture.

questions.question: Why does the chapter emphasize flexible and reversible architectural decisions?
options: Flexible decisions eliminate all technical trade-offs.
Reversible decisions guarantee that no architecture will ever need maintenance.
The world and business needs change, so reversible choices make it easier to adjust course as new information appears.
Reversible decisions are useful only for software licensing.
questions.explanation: The chapter connects reversibility to changing conditions and reducing the risk of architectural decisions.

questions.question: What is a one-way door?
options: A system with only one network endpoint.
A decision that is extremely difficult or nearly impossible to reverse.
A security policy that permits only one user.
A decision that can be changed immediately with no cost.
questions.explanation: The chapter uses Bezos's terminology for decisions that are almost impossible to reverse.

questions.question: What is a two-way door?
options: A physical architecture with two network paths.
A decision that can be reversed relatively easily if it does not work out.
A decision that always requires executive approval.
A decision that permanently locks an organization into one vendor.
questions.explanation: Two-way doors are reversible decisions that allow organizations to iterate and learn.

questions.question: Why should large architecture initiatives often be broken into smaller changes?
options: Breaking work into pieces guarantees zero downtime.
Small changes eliminate the need for architecture.
Large initiatives cannot contain technical dependencies.
Smaller changes can make the overall initiative more manageable and keep individual decisions more reversible.
questions.explanation: The chapter connects change management with breaking large initiatives into smaller, more reversible actions.

questions.question: What is the chapter's main warning about technical solutions?
options: Technical solutions should support business goals rather than exist for their own sake.
Technical sophistication should always take priority over business requirements.
The newest technology is automatically the highest-value solution.
Architecture should be designed independently of business stakeholders.
questions.explanation: The chapter repeatedly stresses that technical solutions exist to support business goals.

questions.question: Which set contains examples of physical or practical constraints that architecture must account for?
options: Only dashboard performance.
Latency, reliability, density, energy consumption, complexity, and budgets.
Only programming language syntax.
Only cloud-provider branding.
questions.explanation: The chapter notes physical limits such as latency and energy plus practical limits such as complexity and budgets.

questions.question: What does it mean to say that good data architecture is 'a living, breathing thing'?
options: Architecture should never be documented.
Architecture should be replaced completely every year.
Architecture exists only while a project is being built.
Architecture must evolve as business needs, technologies, and practices change.
questions.explanation: The chapter says architecture is never finished because change and evolution are central to its purpose.

questions.question: Which characteristic is most associated with bad data architecture in the chapter?
options: Rigid, tightly coupled, overly centralized design that makes development and change harder.
Reversible technology choices.
Flexible components with clear boundaries.
Reusable common components with appropriate security.
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly contrasts good architecture with rigid, tightly coupled, overly centralized designs.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the chapter's nine principles of good data engineering architecture?
options: Maximize architectural complexity.
Plan for failure.
Centralize every domain permanently.
Eliminate all managed services.
questions.explanation: Planning for failure is one of the nine principles listed in the chapter.

questions.question: Which set contains the chapter's nine principles of good data engineering architecture?
options: Choose common components wisely; plan for failure; architect for scalability; architecture is leadership; always be architecting; build loosely coupled systems; make reversible decisions; prioritize security; embrace FinOps.
Build monoliths; use only batch; avoid domains; maximize RTO; eliminate APIs; use fixed capacity; ignore cost.
Use only open source; require one database; avoid abstractions; never refactor; eliminate governance; minimize documentation; ignore failure.
Use one vendor; avoid automation; maximize coupling; centralize everything; eliminate observability; minimize security; avoid cloud.
questions.explanation: These are the nine architecture principles presented in the chapter.

questions.question: Which item is an AWS Well-Architected Framework pillar mentioned in the chapter?
options: Data as a product.
Federated computational governance.
Domain ownership.
Cost optimization.
questions.explanation: The AWS pillars include operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability.

questions.question: Which item is one of Google Cloud's cloud-native architecture principles cited in the chapter?
options: Require physical servers.
Centralize every workload.
Avoid all automation.
Favor managed services.
questions.explanation: Google Cloud's cited principles include designing for automation, being smart with state, and favoring managed services.

questions.question: Why are common components valuable in a large organization?
options: They force every team to solve identical problems independently.
They eliminate the need for permissions.
They can facilitate collaboration, reduce silos, and let teams reuse shared capabilities and knowledge.
They make domain-specific requirements irrelevant.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes common components as a fabric that facilitates collaboration and breaks down silos.

questions.question: Which is an example of a common component discussed in the chapter?
options: Only proprietary hardware purchased for one project.
Only application user interfaces.
Only individual analysts' spreadsheets.
Object storage, version control, observability, orchestration, or processing engines.
questions.explanation: The chapter lists these types of shared capabilities as common components.

questions.question: Why should common components not become one-size-fits-all mandates?
options: Shared components are useful only when nobody uses them.
Forcing every team into one technology can hinder productivity on domain-specific problems.
Domain-specific problems disappear when a central team chooses the tools.
One-size-fits-all designs are always more flexible.
questions.explanation: The chapter advocates common components while warning against forcing inappropriate technology choices on every team.

questions.question: How does separating compute and storage in cloud systems support common components?
options: It forces every workload to use the same compute engine.
A shared storage layer can be accessed by specialized compute or query tools suited to different use cases.
It makes distributed systems impossible.
It eliminates the need for storage permissions.
questions.explanation: The chapter uses cloud compute/storage separation as an example of reusable shared infrastructure.

questions.question: What does 'availability' mean in the chapter?
options: The percentage of time an IT service or component is in an operable state.
The maximum acceptable data loss.
The probability that a system meets requirements during a specified interval.
The amount of data a system can store.
questions.explanation: Availability is defined as the percentage of time a service or component is operable.

questions.question: What does 'reliability' mean in the chapter?
options: The maximum time a service may be offline.
The probability that a system meets defined standards while performing its intended function during a specified interval.
The percentage of time a service has an IP address.
The number of users a system can support.
questions.explanation: The chapter defines reliability in terms of meeting specified performance or functional standards over an interval.

questions.question: What is a recovery time objective (RTO)?
options: The number of replicas required.
The maximum acceptable amount of data loss.
The percentage of uptime required.
The maximum acceptable time for a service or system outage.
questions.explanation: RTO measures acceptable downtime.

questions.question: What is a recovery point objective (RPO)?
options: The maximum acceptable data loss after a failure.
The amount of compute capacity available after scaling.
The maximum acceptable service outage.
The time required to deploy a new service.
questions.explanation: RPO describes the acceptable state after recovery in terms of data loss.

questions.question: Why should RTO be determined partly by business impact?
options: RTO is only a technical measurement with no business relationship.
Different systems have different consequences when unavailable, so acceptable downtime varies by business importance.
RTO is always determined by database size.
RTO must be identical across an organization.
questions.explanation: The chapter gives different RTO examples for an internal reporting system and a public e-commerce site.

questions.question: What is scalability?
options: The ability to eliminate all operational costs.
The percentage of time a system is available.
The ability to increase system capacity to improve performance or handle greater demand.
The maximum acceptable data loss.
questions.explanation: The chapter defines scalability as increasing capacity to handle demand.

questions.question: What is elasticity?
options: The ability to move data between domains without APIs.
The ability to permanently increase hardware capacity.
The ability of a scalable system to dynamically scale up and down based on workload.
The ability to guarantee zero downtime.
questions.explanation: Elasticity refers to dynamic scaling, ideally automatically, in response to current workload.

questions.question: Why is scaling down important in cloud architecture?
options: Scaling down is needed only for on-premises hardware.
Removing unneeded capacity can reduce costs after a workload spike subsides.
Scaling down increases the amount of idle capacity.
Scaling down guarantees higher latency.
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly links scaling down with saving cloud costs.

questions.question: What does 'scale to zero' mean?
options: A system has zero latency.
A system requires no storage.
A system can shut down completely when it is not being used.
A system has zero capacity at all times.
questions.explanation: The chapter uses serverless functions and serverless OLAP databases as examples of systems that can scale to zero.

questions.question: Why can an overly complicated scaling strategy be a poor architectural choice?
options: A simple relational database can never be appropriate.
Complexity always improves reliability.
It can add unnecessary complexity and cost when a simpler design would meet the actual load.
Scaling strategies have no effect on cost.
questions.explanation: The chapter warns against inappropriate scaling strategies and recommends measuring actual and expected load.

questions.question: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?
options: Vertical scaling adds machines; horizontal scaling adds CPU to one machine.
Vertical scaling adds resources to a single machine; horizontal scaling adds more machines.
They are identical terms.
Vertical scaling applies only to cloud systems.
questions.explanation: The chapter distinguishes scaling up a single machine from adding machines to a distributed system.

questions.question: Why can horizontal scaling improve availability and reliability?
options: Workloads can be distributed across multiple machines with redundancy so another machine can continue if one fails.
It eliminates every possible failure.
It prevents replication.
It requires a single machine to handle every request.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes distributed systems as increasing capacity, availability, and reliability through distribution and redundancy.

questions.question: What is a shared-nothing architecture?
options: All requests must run on one central server.
All data must be stored in one database.
Each node handles requests without sharing resources such as memory, disk, or CPU with other nodes.
Every node shares all resources with every other node.
questions.explanation: The chapter defines shared-nothing systems around isolated node resources.

questions.question: What is a shared-disk architecture?
options: Only one node can ever process a request.
Every node has completely isolated storage with no shared resources.
Nodes share access to disk and memory resources so data remains accessible across nodes.
It is a synonym for serverless computing.
questions.explanation: The chapter contrasts shared-disk systems with shared-nothing systems.

questions.question: What is a domain in the chapter's architecture discussion?
options: A real-world subject area or sphere of knowledge, influence, or activity being represented in the architecture.
A single database table.
A physical server rack.
A cloud billing account.
questions.explanation: Domains represent real-world subject areas such as sales or accounting.

questions.question: What is a service?
options: A set of functionality whose goal is to accomplish a particular task.
A complete enterprise architecture.
A storage tier used only for archival data.
A business domain containing every possible function.
questions.explanation: The chapter defines a service as functionality focused on accomplishing a task.

questions.question: Can multiple services exist inside one domain?
options: No; every domain must contain exactly one service.
Yes; a domain can contain multiple services that support different tasks within that subject area.
Only cloud providers can define multiple services.
Services must always belong to different domains.
questions.explanation: The chapter gives a sales domain with orders, invoicing, and products as examples.

questions.question: Why does the chapter recommend talking with users and stakeholders when defining domains and services?
options: User input is needed only after deployment.
Architecture can otherwise be designed only from database schemas.
Stakeholders are responsible for choosing all infrastructure.
Their real-world needs help reveal what the domain should contain and which services will actually help them.
questions.explanation: The chapter warns against architecting in a vacuum and recommends listening to users and stakeholders.

questions.question: What is the key trade-off in tight versus loose coupling?
options: The two approaches have no meaningful trade-offs.
Tight coupling always improves scalability.
Tight coupling can simplify coordination but creates dependencies; loose coupling improves independence but requires standards and accountability to keep data usable.
Loose coupling always removes all complexity.
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly describes trade-offs between centralized dependence and decentralized independence.

questions.question: What is a major benefit of loose coupling?
options: A single central team controls all releases.
Components can evolve more independently because internal implementation details are hidden behind stable interfaces.
Teams must directly access one another's databases.
Every component must be released together.
questions.explanation: Loose coupling allows components and teams to evolve without requiring global changes.

questions.question: What is a potential risk of loose coupling at the organizational level?
options: Decentralized teams may create data that is difficult for peers to use unless common standards, ownership, and accountability exist.
It prevents domain ownership.
It removes the need for governance.
It guarantees identical schemas across every team.
questions.explanation: The chapter warns that decentralization can reduce interoperability without shared standards and accountability.

questions.question: What is a single-tier architecture?
options: An architecture in which every service is independently deployed.
An architecture in which the database and application are tightly coupled, often on a single server.
An architecture based on a shared event bus.
An architecture with separate data, application, and presentation layers.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes single-tier architecture as tightly coupling database and application on one server.

questions.question: Why is single-tier architecture often acceptable for prototypes but not production?
options: Single-tier systems always cost more than distributed systems.
A failure of the shared server, database, or application can take down the entire architecture.
Single-tier systems cannot run locally.
Single-tier systems cannot store data.
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly recommends single-tier designs for testing/prototyping but not production.

questions.question: Why can querying a production application database for analytics be risky?
options: Production databases cannot execute queries.
Analytics workloads can overwhelm the production database and make the application unavailable.
Analytics queries automatically disable replication.
Analytics queries always delete production data.
questions.explanation: The chapter warns that analytics queries against production databases can consume resources needed by the application.

questions.question: What is a multitier architecture?
options: An architecture with no separation of concerns.
An architecture that separates concerns into layers such as data, application logic, and presentation.
A storage-only architecture.
An architecture in which all functionality runs in one codebase on one machine.
questions.explanation: Multitier architecture separates data, application, business logic, presentation, and related concerns.

questions.question: What is a major benefit of a three-tier architecture?
options: Every tier must use the same technology.
The presentation layer must directly access database internals.
All tiers share the same process and memory.
Each tier can be isolated so technologies and concerns can evolve with less monolithic coupling.
questions.explanation: The chapter highlights separation of concerns and freedom to use different technologies within tiers.

questions.question: What is technical coupling versus domain coupling?
options: They are identical concepts.
Technical coupling concerns architectural tiers, while domain coupling concerns how business domains are coupled together.
Technical coupling concerns business ownership, while domain coupling concerns CPU usage.
Both refer only to network latency.
questions.explanation: The chapter distinguishes these two forms of coupling explicitly.

questions.question: Why does a monolith become difficult to change as it grows?
options: Tightly coupled components can produce cascading consequences, making changes and upgrades difficult to isolate.
Every monolith has perfect modularity.
Monoliths eliminate dependencies.
Monoliths automatically create independent services.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes monolithic coupling as making component changes an exercise in trading one problem for another.

questions.question: What is a microservices architecture in the chapter's framing?
options: A centralized database with no service boundaries.
Separate, decentralized, loosely coupled services, each focused on a specific function.
A single application with every function in one codebase.
A system in which every service shares internal implementation details.
questions.explanation: The chapter contrasts microservices with monoliths as decentralized and loosely coupled.

questions.question: What does the chapter recommend when breaking apart a monolith?
options: Never involve stakeholders from the existing monolith.
Move every function into one new central service.
Always rewrite the entire system immediately.
Break out services incrementally rather than automatically attempting a complete refactor all at once.
questions.explanation: The chapter recommends extracting services and getting stakeholder buy-in rather than undertaking an indiscriminate full refactor.

questions.question: What is a noisy neighbor problem in a multitenant system?
options: Heavy usage by one tenant can degrade performance for other tenants sharing the system.
A tenant has no network connection.
Tenants use different cloud providers.
One tenant deletes another tenant's data.
questions.explanation: The chapter defines noisy neighbors in terms of performance degradation caused by one tenant's high usage.

questions.question: What are the two major multitenancy concerns identified in the chapter?
options: Performance and security.
Storage format and SQL syntax.
Cost and programming language.
Batching and machine learning.
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly identifies performance and security as the two key multitenancy factors.

questions.question: Why can multitenant tables be acceptable in some architectures?
options: Tenant isolation is irrelevant when data is shared.
Data can be isolated through appropriate views or other controls, provided those controls cannot leak data.
Views make permissions unnecessary.
Shared tables automatically guarantee perfect security.
questions.explanation: The chapter says multitenant tables can be acceptable when properly isolated, but warns about leakage.

questions.question: What is an event in an event-driven architecture?
options: A database schema definition.
A scheduled batch job.
Something that happened, typically representing a change in the state of something.
A user permission.
questions.explanation: The chapter defines events broadly as occurrences or state changes, such as creating or updating an order.

questions.question: What are the three main areas of an event-driven workflow?
options: Modeling, training, and serving.
Storage, transformation, and deletion.
Event production, routing, and consumption.
Security, governance, and FinOps.
questions.explanation: The chapter breaks an event-driven workflow into production, routing, and consumption.

questions.question: Why should producers, routers, and consumers in an event-driven workflow avoid tight dependencies?
options: Loose dependencies prevent multiple consumers.
Loose dependencies allow components to operate and evolve more independently.
Tight dependencies are required for every event-driven system.
Avoiding dependencies eliminates the need for events.
questions.explanation: The chapter specifically states that event-driven workflows should avoid tightly coupled dependencies among producer, router, and consumer.

questions.question: What is an advantage of event-driven architecture when a service goes offline?
options: Events can only be consumed by the failed service.
The entire architecture must stop.
Event state can be distributed so other services or consumers can still access relevant events.
All events are automatically deleted.
questions.explanation: The chapter highlights resilience and multiple-consumer access as benefits of distributing event state.

questions.question: What is a brownfield architecture project?
options: A project starting from a completely clean slate.
A project that never changes existing systems.
A project that uses only greenfield cloud services.
A project that refactors or reorganizes an existing architecture and must account for legacy constraints.
questions.explanation: Brownfield projects work within the constraints of existing and historical architectural choices.

questions.question: Why does a brownfield project require understanding the existing architecture's history?
options: Past decisions and constraints may explain current behavior and reveal risks, dependencies, and viable migration paths.
Understanding history prevents any architectural change.
Legacy systems never contain useful business value.
History is irrelevant once a new tool is selected.
questions.explanation: The chapter encourages empathy and context rather than simply criticizing previous decisions.

questions.question: What is the strangler pattern?
options: A method for preventing all legacy changes.
A complete rewrite performed in one release.
A database compression technique.
A migration approach in which new systems incrementally replace components of a legacy architecture over time.
questions.explanation: The chapter presents the strangler pattern as an incremental alternative to a risky big-bang rewrite.

questions.question: Why does the chapter favor the strangler pattern over a big-bang rewrite in many brownfield cases?
options: It eliminates all migration planning.
It allows targeted, incremental replacement while assessing impacts and preserving reversibility.
It requires no understanding of the existing system.
It guarantees that legacy systems can be deleted immediately.
questions.explanation: Incremental replacement reduces risk and makes it easier to evaluate the effects of deprecating individual components.

questions.question: What is a greenfield architecture project?
options: A project that cannot use new technologies.
A project that must preserve every legacy component.
A project limited to refactoring existing databases.
A project starting relatively unconstrained by the history and legacy of a prior architecture.
questions.explanation: Greenfield projects begin with a fresh architectural context.

questions.question: What is shiny object syndrome in a greenfield project?
options: Using managed services to reduce complexity.
Choosing fashionable technologies because they are new or exciting without first understanding their impact on project value.
Selecting mature tools based on requirements.
Incrementally replacing a legacy component.
questions.explanation: The chapter warns that greenfield freedom can encourage technology choices driven by novelty rather than requirements.

questions.question: What is resume-driven development?
options: Writing a professional resume for a data engineer.
Developing software from business requirements first.
Using only technologies that have long-term support.
Stacking impressive technologies into a project without prioritizing the project's ultimate goals.
questions.explanation: The chapter uses resume-driven development as a warning against technology choices made for prestige rather than value.

questions.question: What should architects prioritize in both brownfield and greenfield projects?
options: A complete rewrite regardless of risk.
Maximum architectural complexity.
Requirements, trade-offs, flexible and reversible decisions, and positive ROI.
The newest tools regardless of requirements.
questions.explanation: The chapter gives these as the common tenets of good architecture for both project types.

questions.question: What is a data warehouse in the chapter's architecture examples?
options: A device gateway for IoT sensors.
A central data hub used for reporting and analysis, typically containing highly structured data.
A message queue used only for streaming.
A source application database used exclusively for transactions.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes a data warehouse as a central hub for reporting and analysis with structured data.

questions.question: What was Bill Inmon's classic description of a data warehouse intended to emphasize?
options: A customer-facing application database.
A subject-oriented, integrated, nonvolatile, time-variant collection supporting management decisions.
A write-only object store for unstructured data.
A transient event queue for real-time applications.
questions.explanation: The chapter cites Inmon's classic definition of a warehouse.

questions.question: Why is separating OLAP from production OLTP databases valuable?
options: It forces all queries to run on the production database.
It moves analytical load away from production systems and can improve analytics performance and application availability.
It eliminates the need for a warehouse.
It guarantees that analytics never need transformation.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls the separation critical as businesses grow because it protects production systems from analytical workloads.

questions.question: What is MPP in the context of data warehouse architecture?
options: A method for manually loading spreadsheets.
A data privacy regulation.
A business ownership model.
A technical architecture approach involving massively parallel processing.
questions.explanation: The chapter identifies MPP as an example of the technical nature of a data warehouse architecture.

questions.question: Can an organization have a data warehouse without an MPP system?
options: No; a warehouse is defined solely by MPP.
Yes; organizational warehouse architecture and technical MPP architecture are related but not identical.
Only in an on-premises environment.
Only if the warehouse contains unstructured data.
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly notes that a company can have a data warehouse without MPP and vice versa.

questions.question: What is a data lake's key historical appeal?
options: It requires all data to be modeled before storage.
It eliminates all governance requirements.
It can provide flexible, inexpensive storage for varied data on object storage without requiring the highly structured model of a traditional warehouse.
It can store only relational tables.
questions.explanation: The chapter's discussion of lake architecture emphasizes flexible object storage and contrasts it with highly structured warehouses.

questions.question: What problem characterized many first-generation data lakes?
options: They were unable to store unstructured data.
They could become poorly managed data swamps with weak cataloging, painful updates/deletes, and operational complexity.
They eliminated all compliance concerns.
They required every dataset to be fully modeled before ingestion.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes these as major shortcomings of early data lakes.

questions.question: What key capability does a lakehouse add to the traditional data lake model?
options: The elimination of analytical query engines.
A requirement that all data be stored in application databases.
The removal of object storage.
Warehouse-style data management capabilities such as ACID transactions on object storage.
questions.explanation: The chapter highlights ACID transactions as a major departure from the original write-oriented lake model.

questions.question: Why can ACID transactions be valuable in a data lake?
options: They force every workload to be streaming.
They support more reliable updates and deletes and make lake data behave more like managed database data.
They prevent all data from being queried.
They eliminate the need for object storage.
questions.explanation: The chapter contrasts transaction-capable lakehouses with the original write-only lake design.

questions.question: What is Lambda architecture?
options: A three-tier application architecture.
A data governance framework.
An architecture with separate batch, streaming, and serving systems whose results must be reconciled.
An architecture using only a single stream processor.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes Lambda as separate batch and streaming paths plus a serving layer.

questions.question: Why can Lambda architecture be difficult to maintain?
options: Multiple systems and codebases can create reconciliation problems and make code and data harder to keep consistent.
It requires no transformations.
It cannot process historical data.
It uses no separate systems.
questions.explanation: The chapter criticizes Lambda for the complexity of managing multiple independent paths.

questions.question: What is Kappa architecture's central idea?
options: Use a stream-processing platform as the backbone for ingestion, storage, and serving, with replay supporting batch-like processing.
Use separate batch and streaming systems permanently.
Use only a traditional relational database.
Replace all event processing with scheduled SQL.
questions.explanation: Kappa was proposed as a response to Lambda's multiple-code-path complexity.

questions.question: Why has Kappa not been widely adopted according to the chapter?
options: Kappa cannot process real-time data.
Kappa cannot scale to large volumes.
Streaming can be difficult to execute, and Kappa architectures can be complex and expensive in practice.
Kappa requires physical tapes.
questions.explanation: The chapter identifies streaming complexity and cost as reasons for limited Kappa adoption.

questions.question: What is the Dataflow model's key abstraction?
options: Treat all data as events and perform aggregation over windows.
Treat every batch as a separate database.
Treat streaming and batch as unrelated systems.
Treat all data as static tables only.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes Dataflow as viewing all data as events and using windows for aggregation.

questions.question: How does the Dataflow model relate batch and streaming?
options: Streaming is treated as a special kind of static table.
Batch data cannot be represented as events.
Unbounded event streams represent ongoing data, while batches are bounded event streams with natural boundaries.
Batch and streaming require completely different abstractions.
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly frames batches as bounded event streams.

questions.question: What is a tumbling window?
options: A physical storage tier.
A window that always contains the entire history.
A type of database replica.
A window that divides a stream into distinct, non-overlapping intervals for aggregation.
questions.explanation: The chapter mentions tumbling and sliding windows as choices for real-time aggregation.

questions.question: What is a sliding window?
options: A window that moves through a stream over time and can overlap successive intervals.
A window that never changes boundaries.
A network security boundary.
A warehouse partitioning scheme.
questions.explanation: Sliding windows are one of the real-time aggregation window types mentioned in the chapter.

questions.question: Why is the Dataflow approach attractive for unified batch and streaming?
options: The same system and nearly identical code can support both bounded and unbounded event processing.
It eliminates all windowing concepts.
It only works with historical data.
It requires separate codebases for every mode.
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes common abstractions and nearly identical code for batch and streaming.

questions.question: What is an IoT device in the chapter's definition?
options: Only a smartphone application.
A batch processing cluster.
A connected physical device that senses its environment and collects and transmits data.
Only a cloud database.
questions.explanation: The chapter defines IoT as distributed connected devices such as sensors, smart devices, and computers.

questions.question: Why can IoT devices be challenging for data architecture?
options: They never generate data continuously.
They always use identical schemas.
They always have unlimited network connectivity.
They may operate with low power and bandwidth and can experience connectivity disruption, schema differences, corruption, and late-arriving data.
questions.explanation: The chapter lists these operational constraints and data-quality complications for IoT.

questions.question: What is edge computing?
options: Running every workload in a public cloud region.
Archiving data to cold storage.
Processing all data only in a central warehouse.
Processing data on or near the device before sending it downstream.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes devices performing computation on collected data before transmission as edge computing.

questions.question: What is edge machine learning?
options: Running machine-learning processing on or near the device before data is sent downstream.
Training every model in a centralized warehouse.
Using only batch analytics.
Applying security policies at the cloud perimeter.
questions.explanation: The chapter distinguishes edge ML from ordinary edge computation.

questions.question: What is an IoT gateway?
options: A customer-facing BI dashboard.
A machine-learning model.
A hub that connects devices and securely routes data to appropriate destinations.
A data warehouse used for reporting.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes gateways as connection and routing hubs for device swarms.

questions.question: Why can an IoT gateway be valuable for low-power devices?
options: It eliminates the need for any network.
It can provide a way station for data and manage connectivity while allowing devices to use relatively little power.
It forces devices to perform more computation.
It stores all data permanently.
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that gateways can help devices connect using very little power and can retain data temporarily.

questions.question: Why might an IoT gateway upload data in batches?
options: Remote environments may have intermittent connectivity, making periodic upload more practical than continuous transmission.
Batch upload always gives lower latency.
Gateways are incapable of retaining data.
IoT systems cannot produce streams.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes remote gateways that may store data and upload it when connectivity becomes available.

questions.question: What is a notable IoT serving pattern described in the chapter?
options: Use the device only as a data warehouse.
Analyze sensor measurements, derive optimizations, and send results back to devices to reconfigure or improve their operation.
Send every event only to a dashboard and never back to devices.
Archive all sensor data without consumption.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes an IoT reverse-ETL-like pattern in which analytical results are sent back to manufacturing devices.

questions.question: What problem does the data mesh attempt to address?
options: The absence of machine-learning algorithms.
Sprawling centralized data platforms and the divide between operational and analytical data.
The inability of warehouses to run SQL.
The lack of any data storage technology.
questions.explanation: The chapter presents data mesh as a response to monolithic centralized platforms and the operational/analytical divide.

questions.question: What is a core idea of data mesh?
options: All domains must use one physical database.
Domain-oriented decentralized data ownership and architecture.
All governance should be eliminated.
One central team owns every dataset.
questions.explanation: Decentralized domain ownership is the first of the four key data mesh components.

questions.question: Which is one of the four key components of data mesh?
options: Fixed-capacity infrastructure.
Centralized ETL ownership.
Data as a product.
Single-tier architecture.
questions.explanation: Data as a product is explicitly listed among the four components.

questions.question: What does 'self-serve data infrastructure as a platform' mean in data mesh?
options: Only a central team may access data.
Domains are supported by shared platform capabilities that let them produce and consume data without relying entirely on a central data team.
Every domain must build all infrastructure from scratch.
Self-service means eliminating governance.
questions.explanation: The chapter lists self-serve data infrastructure as a platform as a core data mesh component.

questions.question: What is federated computational governance?
options: No governance exists in a data mesh.
Governance is coordinated across domains while supported by computational mechanisms rather than relying solely on a single centralized authority.
Only the cloud provider governs data.
Every domain follows unrelated rules.
questions.explanation: Federated computational governance is the fourth component named in the chapter's data mesh discussion.

questions.question: Why should data engineers remain open-minded about new architecture patterns?
options: The newest architecture is always superior.
One pattern should be adopted universally.
Architecture patterns never change.
New patterns may provide value for particular organizational needs, and no single architecture fits every situation.
questions.explanation: The chapter recommends awareness and open-minded evaluation rather than emotional attachment to one approach.

questions.question: What is the chapter's stance on monoliths versus microservices?
options: Monoliths are always bad.
Architecture should never change after choosing either one.
Microservices are always mandatory.
Use loose coupling as a pragmatic ideal, but recognize that monoliths can be appropriate under some conditions.
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly says monoliths are not necessarily bad and may be a sensible starting point.

questions.question: Why might a small organization intentionally start with a monolith?
options: It can be simpler and faster while the organization is still moving quickly, provided the team plans for future evolution.
A monolith guarantees production reliability.
Monoliths automatically scale better than distributed systems.
Small organizations never need modularity.
questions.explanation: The chapter says starting with a monolith can make sense when moving quickly, but warns against becoming too comfortable with it.

questions.question: What is the modern data stack characterized by in the chapter?
options: A single proprietary platform containing every function.
Only streaming infrastructure.
Physical servers managed entirely in-house.
Plug-and-play, modular, cloud-based components with relatively easy implementation and understandable pricing.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes the modern data stack as modular, cloud-based, and plug-and-play.

questions.question: Why does the chapter caution against becoming emotionally attached to an architecture?
options: Architectural patterns and technologies evolve, so choices should be evaluated by their value for current requirements.
Emotional attachment improves system reliability.
One architecture is guaranteed to remain optimal forever.
Architecture decisions should be made without evidence.
questions.explanation: The chapter encourages awareness of new developments and concrete decisions based on potential value.

questions.question: Who should ideally collaborate with a dedicated data architect?
options: Only database administrators.
No one; architecture should be isolated from engineering.
Data engineers and business stakeholders, among others, because architecture is not designed in a vacuum.
Only cloud vendors.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes data architects working closely with engineers and stakeholders to evaluate trade-offs.

questions.question: When might a data engineer perform architecture duties?
options: Only after becoming a CTO.
In a small or low-data-maturity organization where there may not be a dedicated data architect.
Only in organizations with no data.
Never; data engineers cannot design architecture.
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly says data engineers may work double duty as architects in smaller or less mature companies.

questions.question: Why should data architects work with business stakeholders?
options: Architectural decisions involve trade-offs that must be evaluated against business requirements and value.
Stakeholders eliminate the need for technical analysis.
Business stakeholders should write all infrastructure code.
Architecture has no connection to business outcomes.
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes evaluating architecture trade-offs in the context of business needs.

questions.question: Which question is an example of an architectural trade-off the chapter expects engineers to evaluate?
options: Whether a cloud data warehouse or data lake is more appropriate for the organization's requirements.
Whether business goals should be ignored.
Whether all systems should use the newest technology.
Whether security should be postponed indefinitely.
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly cites warehouse-versus-lake and cloud-platform choices as trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the chapter's overall goal when designing data architecture?
options: Eliminate all architectural change.
Maximize the number of technologies in the stack.
Create an architecture that matches the organization's unique requirements while balancing flexibility, trade-offs, risk, and value.
Find one universal architecture that every company must adopt.
questions.explanation: The chapter concludes by emphasizing organization-specific requirements and careful trade-off analysis.
